title: KV cache offloading: tiers, reload vs recompute, capacity and reuse
summary: How engines keep KV in CPU DRAM, SSD and remote stores, when loading beats prefill, how transfers hide behind compute, how decoding copes when KV does not fit, and how to set up and measure a tier.
outcomes: Explain why the GPU prefix cache runs out and what each offload tier and link (PCIe, shared, NVLink-C2C) adds
Compute load time vs prefill time for a model, prompt length, link bandwidth and GPU throughput
Estimate TTFT with layer-wise loading and explain when overlap helps
Trace how a request's prefix is matched across tiers and engines, and why only a contiguous prefix counts
Choose admission and eviction policies for multi-turn and shared-prefix workloads
Explain how FlexGen, InfiniGen and ShadowKV decode with KV that does not fit in HBM, and which are exact
Show how CacheGen compression and CacheBlend's non-prefix reuse change load-or-recompute decisions
Configure a vLLM or LMCache CPU tier and check hit rate, load bandwidth and TTFT against the cost model

lessons.title: Why the GPU prefix cache runs out, and where KV can go

blocks.md:
Recall what is being cached. In every layer, a transformer turns each token into a key vector and a value vector, K and V, and later tokens attend to them; serving engines keep them in GPU memory as the **KV cache** so they are never computed twice. **Prefill** is the forward pass over the whole prompt that computes the KV of every prompt token at once, before the first output token; **decode** then adds one token per step.

From the PagedAttention course you know that vLLM keeps KV in fixed-size blocks and reuses a cached prefix by hashing full blocks. That reuse has one hard limit: the blocks must still be in **GPU high-bandwidth memory (HBM)**, the memory stacked right next to the GPU chip, very fast but only tens of gigabytes. When HBM fills, the least valuable blocks are evicted and their KV is gone. The next request that needs them pays for a full prefill again.

Workloads that reuse long contexts hit this limit fast. The CachedAttention paper (USENIX ATC 2024, the USENIX Annual Technical Conference) found that 73% of ShareGPT conversations (a public collection of ChatGPT chats that users chose to share) are multi-turn, and that recomputing the history can be up to 99% of prefill cost in later turns. It also estimated that free HBM on its server with four NVIDIA A100 GPUs would fill with KV in about 14 seconds of serving. Agents, retrieval-augmented generation (RAG), which pastes the same retrieved documents into many prompts, and long system prompts show the same pattern: the same prefix comes back, but minutes later, long after HBM evicted it.

**KV cache offloading** keeps evicted (or copied) KV blocks in slower but much larger memory: CPU DRAM (the server's ordinary main memory, also called host memory), a local NVMe SSD (a flash drive attached over PCIe, the bus that links the CPU side to the GPU), or a remote store shared by many servers. A later hit loads those bytes back instead of running prefill again.

Let's size the problem with **Llama 3 8B**, recalled from the LLM inference course: 32 layers, 8 **KV heads** (grouped-query attention, GQA, shares each among 4 query heads) of 128 numbers, BF16 at 2 bytes each. So every token stores $2 \times 32 \times 8 \times 128 \times 2 = 131{,}072$ bytes: 2 for K and V, times 32 layers, times 8 heads, times 128 numbers, times 2 bytes. That is 128 KiB, since a kibibyte is 1,024 bytes, 2 to the 10th; the bi stands for binary. Likewise a gibibyte is 1,024 cubed bytes, about 1.07 GB, so one 8,192-token prompt, 8,192 times 128 KiB, needs exactly one gibibyte.

blocks.title: How many 8K-token prompts of Llama 3 8B KV fit per tier

scenes.caption: At 128 KiB of KV per token, one 8,192-token prompt needs 1 GiB. 40 GB of free HBM holds 37 such prompts; 512 GB of host DRAM holds 476.
A 4 TB SSD holds 3,725. Capacities are assumed round numbers for one server; the point is the gap: about 13x more from HBM to DRAM and 100x to SSD.

blocks.md: A few words for the paths between tiers. Copies between GPU and host memory use **DMA** (direct memory access): the GPU's copy engines move the bytes on their own while its compute cores and the CPU keep working. DMA needs **pinned** (page-locked) host memory, pages the operating system promises never to move or swap out, so the copy engine can rely on their physical addresses; ordinary pageable memory is first staged through a pinned buffer. In CUDA, NVIDIA's GPU programming platform, `cudaMemcpyAsync` queues such a copy and returns at once. **NVIDIA Dynamo** is an open-source framework for serving models across many GPUs; its KV Block Manager (KVBM) manages these tiers.

How fast is the path from host memory to the GPU? On most servers it is one PCIe x16 link per GPU. NVIDIA's product pages quote 64 GB/s for the [A100](https://www.nvidia.com/en-us/data-center/a100/)'s PCIe Gen4 link and 128 GB/s for the [H100](https://www.nvidia.com/en-us/data-center/h100/)'s Gen5 link, counting both directions together, so about 32 and 64 GB/s each way before protocol overhead (Gen4 x16 is 31.5 GB/s after line encoding, the figure used below). Copies achieve less than the peak: vLLM's developers measured about 50 GB/s for one-direction DMA copies on an H100, and 83.4 GB/s when copying both ways at once. That is where the next lesson's 50 GB/s planning number comes from. Only pinned memory gets near these numbers, for the reason in the DMA paragraph above.

Two things move that number by about an order of magnitude, in either direction. First, the link is often **shared**. GPUs, network cards and SSDs hang off PCIe switches, and devices behind one switch share its single uplink to the CPU. NVIDIA measured this on a DGX-2 (16 V100 GPUs, PCIe Gen3): each of its four PCIe trees had one path from system memory, 12 to 12.5 GB/s, so 48 to 50 GB/s for the whole machine. If the four GPUs on one tree reload KV at once, each gets about 3 GB/s.

Second, some machines replace PCIe with a **coherent** CPU-GPU link, one over which the GPU can read CPU memory with ordinary loads and see consistent data. On NVIDIA's Grace Hopper superchip, NVLink-C2C carries 450 GB/s per direction (900 GB/s total) between the GPU and the Grace CPU's LPDDR5X memory, which itself delivers up to 546 GB/s.

blocks.title: Loading one 8K-token prompt's KV (1 GiB) over different paths

scenes.caption: 1,073,741,824 bytes divided by bandwidth: 34.1 ms at the 31.5 GB/s peak of one Gen4 x16 direction, 21.5 ms at the 50 GB/s vLLM measured on an H100.
Four GPUs sharing a 12 GB/s uplink get about 3 GB/s each: 358 ms. That is slower than recomputing the prompt (330 ms at the next lesson's assumed 400 TFLOPS).

At NVLink-C2C's 450 GB/s peak the same GiB takes 2.4 ms, about 9x the measured PCIe copy and 7x Gen5's 64 GB/s peak (achieved C2C rates are lower). The tier is the same DRAM; only the path changed, and with it the load-or-recompute decision.

blocks.title: The KV tier hierarchy and the paths between tiers

scenes.caption: Four tiers, fastest and smallest first. Names differ by system: Dynamo's KV Block Manager calls them G1 to G4, SGLang HiCache calls GPU, host and storage L1, L2 and L3. LMCache instead calls CPU memory L1.
Store path: when a KV block is complete, a copy goes to pinned host memory with an asynchronous DMA (cudaMemcpyAsync in vLLM), overlapping model compute. The GPU copy stays until GPU eviction.
Lower tiers are fed from host memory. In vLLM's tiered spec, secondary tiers (filesystem, object store, peer instances) cannot touch GPU memory, so everything is staged through the CPU tier.
Hit path: a later request whose prefix lives in a lower tier has those blocks promoted back up, through host memory, into GPU blocks, instead of recomputing them with prefill.

Some managers skip the hop: Dynamo's KVBM can onboard a disk block straight into GPU memory through NIXL (NVIDIA's data-transfer library), possibly with GPUDirect Storage, which lets the SSD copy straight into GPU memory. Only the data path changes.

blocks.md: Two different reasons to offload exist. Most of this course is about the first; the capacity lesson covers the second. **Reuse offloading** (LMCache, vLLM's OffloadingConnector, SGLang HiCache, Mooncake, Dynamo KVBM) saves KV so a *future request* can skip prefill. LMCache is an open-source KV cache layer that plugs into vLLM and SGLang, the OffloadingConnector is vLLM's built-in offloader, HiCache is SGLang's hierarchical cache, and Mooncake is the platform behind Moonshot AI's Kimi chatbot. **Capacity offloading** (FlexGen, InfiniGen) keeps the KV of the *current* batch partly in CPU memory during decoding so a bigger batch or longer context fits; FlexGen, a 2023 research system, ran OPT-175B (Meta's open 175-billion-parameter model) on a single 16 GB GPU this way, and InfiniGen prefetches only the KV entries it predicts the next layer will attend to strongly.

Reuse offloading does not make the GPU's attention kernel read from CPU memory. Blocks are copied back into GPU blocks before the kernel runs; the kernel only ever sees HBM. What it buys is skipping the *prefill compute* that would otherwise recreate those blocks. Capacity offloading can differ: FlexGen can run attention on the CPU, where the KV lives.
Each tier down is roughly 10x bigger and slower. Offloading turns a prefix-cache miss into a load from a lower tier, which pays off only if the load is faster than recomputing.

blocks.question: A server runs Llama 3 8B with 40 GB of HBM free for KV and serves 200 users who each come back every few minutes with a growing 8K-token chat history. Without offloading, what happens on most return visits?
options: Prefix caching hits, because vLLM never evicts blocks that another request might reuse
The history was evicted from HBM (only about 37 such histories fit), so prefill recomputes it
The attention kernel reads the history directly from CPU memory over PCIe
The request is rejected until enough HBM is freed
blocks.explain: 200 histories of 1 GiB each cannot fit in 40 GB; only about 37 can. Free blocks are evicted when space is needed, so most returning users miss and pay a full prefill. Offloading to a 512 GB DRAM tier would keep all 200 histories.

blocks.question: Which system is an example of capacity offloading rather than reuse offloading?
options: LMCache storing chunks in Redis for other engines
SGLang HiCache writing radix-tree nodes to host memory
FlexGen placing part of the attention cache in CPU memory during decoding
vLLM's OffloadingConnector copying finished prompt blocks to pinned memory
blocks.explain: FlexGen offloads weights, activations and KV of the running batch to fit a huge model on a small GPU and maximize throughput. The other three save KV so later requests that share the prefix can skip prefill.

lessons.title: Reload or recompute: bytes versus prefill FLOPs

blocks.md: A cache hit in a lower tier is not automatically a win. You can get the KV for a prefix in two ways: **recompute** it by running prefill on the GPU, or **load** the saved bytes over some link. The faster option wins, so we need a cost model for each. We will use Llama 3 8B, BF16, and *stated assumptions* for hardware: the GPU sustains 400 TFLOPS on prefill, 400 trillion floating-point operations (FLOPs) per second, and each tier has an effective bandwidth (host DRAM over PCIe 50 GB/s, an RDMA pool 12 GB/s, local NVMe 6 GB/s, an object store 1 GB/s). These are round planning numbers, not measurements (the first lesson shows where 50 GB/s comes from). RDMA (remote direct memory access) means the network card reads or writes another machine's memory directly, without that machine's CPU copying the data, which is why a remote pool can beat a local SSD. An object store is a bucket service such as Amazon S3, built for capacity rather than speed.

blocks.tex: b_{kv} = 2 \cdot L \cdot h_{kv} \cdot d_h \cdot s = 2 \cdot 32 \cdot 8 \cdot 128 \cdot 2 = 131{,}072 \text{ bytes}, \qquad T_{load}(n) = \frac{n\, b_{kv}}{B}
blocks.caption: Bytes per token: K and V, for L layers, h_kv KV heads of size d_h, s bytes per value. Load time is n tokens times b_kv bytes, divided by the link bandwidth B, so it is linear in the prompt length n.

blocks.tex: T_{rec}(n) \approx \frac{2 P n + 2 L d\, n^2}{F}
blocks.caption: Prefill FLOPs: 2 FLOPs per weight per token (P = 6.98e9 weights in the linear layers of Llama 3 8B), plus causal attention (QK and AV) with d = 4096 query dimensions per layer. F is GPU throughput.

blocks.md: Where the two terms come from. A matrix multiply does one multiply and one add for every weight it touches, so each token costs 2 FLOPs per weight: $2Pn$ for the prompt. $P$ = 6.98e9 counts the weights of the 32 layers' attention projections and feed-forward networks; the rest of the 8 billion is the token embedding table, a lookup rather than a multiply, and the output layer, which prefill only needs for the last token. Attention adds two products per layer: queries times keys (QK) to score each pair of tokens, then the scores times the values (AV). Attention is causal, so each token only attends to itself and earlier tokens: about $n^2/2$ pairs, each a dot product of length $d$ = 4096 (32 query heads times 128), which is $2d$ FLOPs. That gives $d n^2$ for QK, the same for AV, so $2 L d n^2$ over $L$ layers. At 8,192 tokens: 1.14e14 plus 1.76e13 is 1.32e14 FLOPs, divided by $F$, the GPU's FLOPs per second.

The ratio is what matters. Per token, short-prompt prefill costs about $2P = 14$ GFLOPs while the KV is only 131 KB, roughly 100,000 FLOPs per byte. Setting load time equal to recompute time, bytes over bandwidth equal to FLOPs over throughput, and solving for the bandwidth gives the **break-even bandwidth** $B^{\ast} = n\, b_{kv} F / \text{FLOPs}(n)$: any tier faster than $B^{\ast}$ should be read rather than recomputed. For Llama 3 8B at 400 TFLOPS, $B^{\ast}$ is 3.7 GB/s at 1K tokens and 3.3 GB/s at 8K: 1.07e9 bytes times 4e14 FLOPs per second, divided by 1.32e14 FLOPs. The LLM inference course's preemption lesson made the same swap-or-recompute choice for a preempted sequence; here the KV comes back for a new request.

One caution about $F$: it is a *sustained* rate, which a long prefill can reach and a short one cannot. A prefill of a few dozen tokens is memory-bound, as the GPU basics course showed for decode: it still reads every weight, 16 GB for Llama 3 8B, which takes 7.85 ms at the A100's 2,039 GB/s (the decode floor the LLM inference course uses), while the formula says 2.2 ms for 64 tokens at the assumed 400 TFLOPS (2.9 ms at the A100's dense 312). At 1K tokens the formula's 36 ms is a lower bound, reached only if the kernels hold $F$. So for short prompts and short new suffixes the formula underestimates recompute, and loading wins more often than the break-even numbers suggest.

scenes.caption: Prefill of 8,192 tokens costs 1.32e14 FLOPs; at an assumed 400 TFLOPS that is 330 ms. The KV it produces is 1.07 GB.
Loading the same 1.07 GB at assumed effective bandwidths: 21.5 ms from host DRAM at 50 GB/s, 89.5 ms from a remote pool at 12 GB/s, 179 ms from NVMe at 6 GB/s. All beat prefill.
An object store at 1 GB/s needs 1,074 ms, over 3x slower than recomputing. A tier is only worth reading when its bandwidth beats the break-even point, here 3.3 GB/s.

blocks.title: Recompute vs load time as the prompt grows (Llama 3 8B)

scenes.caption: Host DRAM at 50 GB/s: loading is 13x to 79x faster than prefill at every length shown. Both curves rise, but prefill bends upward because attention cost grows with the square of the length.
NVMe at 6 GB/s: still faster than recomputing everywhere (1.6x at 1K tokens, 2.6x at 32K), but the gap is now small.
An object store at 1 GB/s: loading loses until prompts reach about 147K tokens, where quadratic attention finally makes prefill slower than a linear byte copy.
A faster GPU moves the line. At 1,000 TFLOPS, NVMe at 6 GB/s loses to recompute below about 30K tokens; break-even bandwidth rises to 8 to 9 GB/s.

blocks.prompt: Llama 3 70B has 80 layers and also 8 KV heads. Compared with the 8B model, does it need a faster or a slower link before loading beats recomputing?
blocks.reveal: **Slower.** Its KV is $2 \times 80 \times 8 \times 128 \times 2 = 327{,}680$ bytes per token, only 2.5x the 8B model, because grouped-query attention keeps just 8 KV heads. But its linear layers have 6.85e10 weights, about 10x more FLOPs per token. Break-even bandwidth at 8K tokens drops from 3.26 GB/s to 0.89 GB/s. Bigger GQA models are *easier* to offload profitably.

blocks.md: The 400 TFLOPS assumes the GPU is otherwise idle. On a busy server, recomputing a prefix steals compute from every other request in the batch, while a load mostly uses the copy engine and the PCIe or network link. So loading can win even when the TTFT (time to first token) numbers look tied. The reverse also happens: the LMCache paper reports that with a 15 Gbps (gigabits per second, under 2 GB/s) remote store, loading can take longer than prefill for short contexts or small models.

You can also do both. **Cake** (Jin et al., 2024) splits one prefix between the two resources: the GPU computes KV chunks forward from token 0 while an I/O thread loads chunks backward from the end, and they stop where they meet. Later tokens are the expensive ones to compute (they attend to everything before them) but cost the same to load, so loading from the back is the right split. vLLM exposes a simpler knob, `max_load_tokens` (experimental, per request), which caps how many tokens are loaded from offloaded storage; tokens beyond the cap are recomputed.

Compare bytes over bandwidth with FLOPs over throughput. Fast tiers (host DRAM, RDMA pools) beat prefill at almost any length; slow tiers only pay off for long prompts, big models, or a GPU that is busy anyway.

blocks.question: Your NVMe tier delivers 6 GB/s. You upgrade the GPU from 400 to 1,000 effective TFLOPS and keep serving Llama 3 8B with 8K-token prompts. What happens to the case for reading KV from NVMe?
options: It gets stronger: a faster GPU also transfers data faster
Nothing changes: the decision depends only on prompt length
It weakens: recompute drops to 132 ms, while the 179 ms NVMe load stays the same, so recomputing now wins
It weakens only for prompts longer than 32K tokens
blocks.explain: Load time depends on bytes and link bandwidth, not on GPU FLOPs. Prefill time falls from 330 ms to 132 ms with the faster GPU, so the 179 ms NVMe read now loses at 8K tokens. Break-even bandwidth rises to about 8 GB/s, and NVMe only wins above roughly 30K tokens.

blocks.question: A colleague says: 'Prefill cost grows faster than load cost as prompts get longer, so offloading pays off more for long prompts.' Which part of the cost model makes this true?
options: KV bytes per token grow with prompt length
The attention term in prefill grows with $n^2$ while bytes grow with $n$
Longer prompts compress better on disk
PCIe bandwidth increases for larger transfers
blocks.explain: Every token stores the same 131,072 bytes, so load time is linear in $n$. Prefill has the linear-layer term $2Pn$ plus causal attention $2Ldn^2$, which dominates at long lengths. That is why even a 1 GB/s object store beats prefill beyond about 147K tokens in this model.

lessons.title: Hiding the transfer: layer-wise loading and asynchronous saving

blocks.md: A transformer computes one layer at a time, and layer $i$ only needs layer $i$'s KV. So nothing forces us to wait for the whole cache before starting. **Layer-wise loading** uses two CUDA streams (a stream is a queue of GPU work that runs in order; work in different streams can run at the same time): a copy stream brings layer $i+1$'s KV into HBM while the compute stream runs layer $i$. CachedAttention calls this layer-wise pre-loading, SGLang HiCache loads layer N+1 while computing layer N, and LMCache gives each layer separate compute and data-movement streams with a buffer that holds only one layer's KV.

blocks.title: Layer-wise loading on a toy 4-layer model

scenes.caption: Naive: load all 4 layers of cached KV (3 ms each), then compute the new tokens layer by layer (2 ms each). The first token waits for the sum: 20 ms.
Layer-wise: layer 0 can start as soon as its own KV has arrived. Compute of layer i overlaps the load of layer i+1. Done at 14 ms: the total load (12) plus one layer of compute (2).
If compute dominates (1 ms load, 3 ms compute per layer), loading hides almost completely: 13 ms is the 12 ms of compute plus one layer of load.
Load-bound again, but a previous job holds the GPU until 6 ms and loading only starts when this job starts. Finish: 20 ms.
CachedAttention's fix: a reserved HBM read buffer lets the first layers preload while the previous job still runs. Here two layers preload during 0 to 6 ms and the job finishes at 14 ms.

blocks.caption: Simplified model with L identical layers: the slower stream sets the pace, and only one layer of the faster stream is left exposed at the start or end.

blocks.md: Now a real-sized example: the second turn of a chat on Llama 3 8B. The first turn left 8,192 tokens of KV (1.07 GB) in host DRAM, and the user adds 512 new tokens. The new tokens cost 9.41e12 FLOPs ($2P$ times 512 is 7.15e12 for the weights, plus 2.27e12 for attention, since each new token scores all 8,192 cached keys and the new tokens before it), which is 23.5 ms at 400 TFLOPS. Spread over 32 layers, each layer has 0.67 ms of loading (21.5 / 32) and 0.73 ms of compute (23.5 / 32). Compute is the slightly slower stream, so the overlap formula gives 23.5 + 0.67 = 24.2 ms. That is this model's TTFT for turn 2. Every TTFT estimate in this course counts only getting the KV and running prefill on an idle GPU; the TTFT of the LLM inference course also includes queueing, which these models leave out.

blocks.title: Turn 2 of a chat: 8,192 cached tokens plus 512 new (Llama 3 8B)

scenes.caption: Without any cache, prefill must process all 8,704 tokens: 353 ms at 400 TFLOPS.
With the history in host DRAM: the 1.07 GB load takes 21.5 ms and the 512 new tokens take 23.5 ms. Run back to back that is 45.0 ms; overlapped layer by layer it is 24.2 ms.
From NVMe at 6 GB/s the load (179 ms) dominates, so overlap only hides the small compute: 202.5 ms sequential vs 179.7 ms layer-wise. Still about 2x better than recomputing.

blocks.prompt: In the NVMe case, layer-wise loading saved only 23 ms out of 202 ms. What would make overlap save more?
blocks.reveal: Overlap can hide at most the *smaller* of the two streams. With 179 ms of load and 23.5 ms of compute, compute is all there is to hide. Overlap helps most when the two are balanced, as in the host DRAM case (21.5 vs 23.5 ms), where it nearly halves TTFT. To speed up the NVMe case you must cut bytes (a faster tier, prefetching to DRAM ahead of time, or KV compression, the subject of a later lesson) rather than overlap more.

blocks.md: CachedAttention states the same condition for when overlap is not enough: if the per-token load time times the history length exceeds the per-token prefill time times the new length, loading is exposed. It reserves an HBM **read buffer** so pre-loading can start while the previous job is still on the GPU. In its ablation, an experiment that removes one component at a time to measure what each contributes (LLaMA-13B, 1K history tokens, 100 new tokens), layer-wise pre-loading without the buffer cut prefill time by 35%, and with a 15-layer buffer by 61%.

Saving runs the other way. **Asynchronous saving** writes KV out to host memory layer by layer while the GPU keeps working, using an HBM write buffer so the next job is not blocked; CachedAttention reports 13% to 15% lower execution time from it. vLLM's OffloadingConnector copies completed blocks into pinned host memory with `cudaMemcpyAsync` as they are produced, and Dynamo's KVBM performs its offloads and onboards asynchronously at the end of the forward pass.

Pinned (page-locked) host memory matters. Asynchronous DMA copies need it; vLLM reserves `cpu_bytes_to_use` bytes of pinned host memory for its CPU tier, and Dynamo's G2 host pool is pinned memory, rather than ordinary pageable buffers.
Overlap turns load plus compute into roughly max(load, compute). It is free speed when the two are balanced and nearly useless when one dominates.

blocks.question: A deployment loads a 2 GB cached prefix at 25 GB/s (80 ms) and computes the new tokens in 10 ms over 40 layers. Using the simplified overlap model, what TTFT should layer-wise loading give?
options: About 90 ms, because overlap cannot help a load-bound case
About 80 ms: the load dominates and only one layer of compute (0.25 ms) is exposed
About 45 ms, because the two streams split the work
About 10 ms, because the load is hidden behind compute
blocks.explain: max(80, 10) + min(80, 10)/40 = 80 + 0.25 ms. All compute hides under the load, but the load itself cannot hide behind anything. Sequential would be 90 ms, so overlap saves the 10 ms of compute and no more.

blocks.question: Why can layer-wise loading start computing layer 0 before layers 1 to 31 of the cached KV have arrived?
options: Because attention at layer 0 only reads layer 0's keys and values
Because the GPU recomputes the missing layers in parallel
Because KV caches are stored layer-interleaved by token
Because the scheduler skips attention for cached tokens
blocks.explain: Each layer's attention uses only the K and V produced at that same layer. Layer 0 needs nothing from deeper layers, so it can run as soon as its own KV is in HBM while later layers are still in flight.

lessons.title: Capacity offloading: decoding with KV that does not fit in HBM

blocks.md:
So far, offloaded KV was a *saved* prefix: copied back into HBM once, then used. Now the other problem from the first lesson: the KV of the requests *currently decoding* does not fit. A tiny example: OPT-30B, Meta's open 30-billion-parameter model, has 48 layers, hidden size 7168 and ordinary multi-head attention (no GQA), so in FP16 each token stores $2 \times 48 \times 7168 \times 2 = 1{,}376{,}256$ bytes of KV, about 10x Llama 3 8B's 128 KiB. One sequence of 512 prompt plus 32 output tokens holds 0.75 GB; a batch of 64 holds 48 GB. Add 59 GB of FP16 weights and a 16 GB GPU is hopeless.

**Capacity offloading** keeps part of the KV (and often the weights) in CPU memory or on disk *during* decoding. The catch: every decode step attends over the whole cache, so a cache in CPU memory must cross PCIe every step, not once per request.

**FlexGen** (Sheng et al., ICML 2023) attacks this for *throughput-oriented* jobs: benchmarks, batch scoring, data processing, where seconds per token are fine if tokens per second is high. The trick is to reuse each loaded weight across many sequences. Picture decoding as a grid of squares, one column per layer (repeated for every generated token) and one row per batch. Going row by row (one batch through all layers, then the next) reloads every layer's weights for each batch. Going down a column reuses one layer's weights for all batches but needs every batch's activations and KV at once. The **zig-zag block schedule** goes down a column for a *block* of several GPU batches, then moves to the next layer, so one weight load serves the whole block. With 2 batches and 3 layers, row by row loads 6 layer weights per token; the zig-zag order (batch 1 layer 1, batch 2 layer 1, batch 1 layer 2, ...) loads 3. FlexGen calls GPU batch size times the number of GPU batches in a block the **effective batch size**, and proves this schedule's I/O is within 2x of optimal.

Where each tensor lives is a search problem. A FlexGen policy has 11 variables: the block size, the GPU batch size, and the percentages of weights ($w_g, w_c, w_d$), activations and KV cache placed on GPU, CPU and disk. FlexGen enumerates a few (block size, GPU batch size) pairs and, for each, solves a **linear program** (an optimization with a linear objective and linear constraints, which solves quickly) over the nine placement percentages, minimizing the predicted time per sequence (the block's total time divided by the block size) from a cost model of compute and of every transfer, subject to each device's memory capacity.

On a T4 GPU (16 GB) with 208 GB of DRAM, a 1.5 TB SSD and a 12 GB/s GPU-CPU link, its OPT-30B policy put 20% of the weights on the GPU, 80% on the CPU, all activations and KV on the CPU, with GPU batches of 48 and 3 per block (effective batch 144). It generated 7.32 tokens/s; the same engine with DeepSpeed's placement policy reached 1.57.

blocks.tex: \text{PCIe bytes per token} \approx \frac{W_{cpu}}{b} + \begin{cases} K\!V_{seq} & \text{attention on GPU} \\ a_{seq} & \text{attention on CPU} \end{cases}
blocks.caption: Per generated token: the CPU-resident weights W_cpu are shared by the b sequences of a block, but each sequence's own KV (or, with attention on the CPU, its much smaller activations) crosses the link every step.

blocks.code:
# OPT-30B decode with weights mostly on CPU and the KV cache on CPU (FlexGen's
# OPT-30B policy: 20% of weights on GPU, 80% on CPU, all KV on CPU).
# Byte formulas from the FlexGen paper (FP16): weights per layer 8*h1^2 + 4*h1*h2,
# KV per layer per sequence 4*h1*(s + n/2) on average, activations 4*h1 per layer.
l, h1, h2 = 48, 7168, 28672          # OPT-30B: layers, hidden, FFN hidden
s, n = 512, 32                       # prompt and output length (FlexGen's setting)
pcie = 12e9                          # GPU-CPU link in FlexGen's T4 machine
w_cpu = 0.8 * l * (8*h1**2 + 4*h1*h2)    # weight bytes streamed per decode step
kv_seq = l * 4*h1*(s + n/2)              # KV bytes per sequence per step
act_seq = l * 4*h1                        # activation bytes per sequence per step
print(f"weights from CPU per step: {w_cpu/1e9:.1f} GB")
print(f"KV per sequence per step:  {kv_seq/1e6:.0f} MB; activations {act_seq/1e6:.2f} MB")
for b in (1, 64, 144):
    gpu_attn = w_cpu/b + kv_seq          # bytes over PCIe per generated token
    cpu_attn = w_cpu/b + act_seq
    print(f"batch {b:3d}: GPU attention {gpu_attn/1e9:6.2f} GB/token "
          f"({gpu_attn/pcie*1e3:7.1f} ms), CPU attention {cpu_attn/1e9:6.2f} GB/token "
          f"({cpu_attn/pcie*1e3:7.1f} ms)")
blocks.caption: Runs on any CPU with Python 3 and no packages. Byte formulas are FlexGen's (FP16); the link is its T4 machine's 12 GB/s. Output is in the next block.

blocks.md:
Its output:

```
weights from CPU per step: 47.4 GB
KV per sequence per step:  727 MB; activations 1.38 MB
batch   1: GPU attention  48.08 GB/token ( 4006.6 ms), CPU attention  47.35 GB/token ( 3946.1 ms)
batch  64: GPU attention   1.47 GB/token (  122.2 ms), CPU attention   0.74 GB/token (   61.8 ms)
batch 144: GPU attention   1.06 GB/token (   88.0 ms), CPU attention   0.33 GB/token (   27.5 ms)
```

At batch 1, streaming 47 GB of weights per token takes 4 seconds a token. Batching divides that weight traffic, but not the KV: at batch 64 the two are already equal, and at 144 the KV is over two thirds of the bytes.

blocks.title: One layer of OPT-30B decode over a 12 GB/s link (FlexGen policy)

scenes.caption: Batch 1: this layer's 0.99 GB of CPU-resident weights take 82 ms; one sequence's KV adds 1.3 ms. Times 48 layers, about 4 s per token. Compute is drawn as a sliver (simplified, not measured).

Zig-zag block of 3 GPU batches of 48: one weight load now serves 144 sequences, but each batch's KV for this layer (48 x 15.1 MB = 727 MB, 60.6 ms) still crosses. Per token: 263.9 ms x 48 layers / 144 = 88 ms.

Attention on the CPU: the KV never moves, only 0.34 ms of activations. The link now carries 82.6 ms per layer, 27.5 ms per token. The CPU's attention time is not drawn; it is real, as FlexGen's measurements show.

blocks.md: That third scene is FlexGen's **CPU delegation**. With the KV on the CPU, attention on the GPU must move $b \times s \times h_1 \times 4$ bytes per layer (batch, sequence length, hidden size, 2 bytes each for K and V), while attention on the CPU only moves the activations, $b \times h_1 \times 4$ bytes: $s$ times less. FlexGen therefore computes attention on the CPU for long sequences ($s \geq 512$) whenever the KV is not on the GPU. Bytes alone predict 3.2x (88 to 27.5 ms per token); FlexGen's ablation measured 1.8x, 4.03 tokens/s without CPU compute against 7.32 with it, because the CPU's attention time and the prefill also count. FlexGen turns delegation off when it compresses KV to 4 bits, since decompressing on the CPU costs too much.

blocks.prompt: An interactive chatbot serves one user at a time with the same OPT-30B setup. Would moving attention to the CPU fix its latency?
blocks.reveal: **No.** At batch 1 the weights are 47.4 of the 48.1 GB per token, so CPU attention only trims it to 47.35 GB: still about 4 seconds per token. Throughput-style capacity offloading pays only when a big block of sequences shares each weight load. Interactive serving needs the weights in HBM and a way to move *less KV*, which is what the next two systems do.

blocks.md: **InfiniGen** (Lee et al., OSDI 2024) keeps the full KV pool in CPU memory and fetches only the tokens that matter. Its observation: the input to layer $i$ is very similar to the input to layer $i-1$. So while layer $i-1$ runs, it multiplies layer $i-1$'s attention input by a *partial* query weight and a *partial* key cache of layer $i$ (30% of the columns) to guess layer $i$'s attention scores, then prefetches the KV of tokens whose guessed score is within $\alpha$ of the maximum. Subtracting $\alpha$ before softmax divides the weight by $e^{\alpha}$, so with $\alpha = 4$ a skipped token has under 1/54 of the top token's weight. Offline, it rotates the query and key weight matrices by an orthogonal matrix from an SVD (a matrix factorization), which leaves $QK^\top$ unchanged but concentrates large values in a few columns, so 30% of the columns predict well. With $\alpha$ of 4 or 5 it used under 10% of the KV on average.

On an RTX A6000 over PCIe 3.0 x16 with OPT-13B, 1,920 input tokens and batch 20, InfiniGen was 1.63x to 32.93x faster than its baselines (FlexGen with full FP16 KV, 4-bit KV, H2O token eviction and CUDA unified memory).

**ShadowKV** (Sun et al., 2024) targets long contexts. It keeps a low-rank copy (rank 160) of the *pre-RoPE* keys on the GPU, that is, keys before rotary position embedding (RoPE) rotates them. RoPE rotates pairs of key coordinates by an angle that depends on the token's position, and ShadowKV found the keys most low-rank before that rotation. It moves the values to CPU memory. For each 8-token chunk it keeps a **landmark**, the mean of the chunk's keys. Each decode step scores chunks against the landmarks, picks the top ones (a 1.56% budget: 256 chunks of 8 tokens at 128K), fetches just those values from the CPU and rebuilds their keys from the low-rank factors while the values travel. A few outlier chunks (0.2 to 0.3%) that landmarks approximate badly stay on the GPU. On an A100 with Llama-3.1-8B it supported up to 6x larger batches and 3.04x higher throughput.

Exactness differs. Reuse offloading and FlexGen without compression are exact: every key and value is used. InfiniGen and ShadowKV *approximate* attention by skipping tokens judged unimportant, so they are judged on accuracy benchmarks as well as speed. The same selection idea also works for KV that stays in HBM (Quest, H2O), to read or keep fewer tokens.

Capacity offloading moves KV every decode step, so it pays only when each crossing is amortized (a big block of sequences sharing each weight load) or shrunk (attention computed where the KV lives, or only the important tokens fetched).

blocks.question: Two jobs have KV that does not fit in one GPU: an overnight job scoring a million documents with a 30B model, and an interactive assistant with 128K-token contexts that must stream tokens quickly. Which designs fit?
options: FlexGen-style offloading for both, with the largest effective batch that fits
Sparse fetching (InfiniGen, ShadowKV) for the overnight job; FlexGen-style batching for the assistant
FlexGen-style batching with weights and KV on the CPU for the overnight job; sparse fetching with accuracy checks for the assistant
Neither: offloading only helps when a later request reuses a prefix
blocks.explain: The overnight job only cares about tokens per second, so a large block that shares each weight load (and CPU attention) is ideal. The assistant cannot wait seconds per token at small batch, so its weights stay in HBM and it fetches only the KV that matters, checking that skipping tokens does not hurt answers.

blocks.question: With attention on the GPU, raising FlexGen's effective batch from 64 to 144 cut PCIe bytes per token only from 1.47 to 1.06 GB, not by 144/64. Why?
options: Each sequence's KV still crosses the link every step, and that part does not shrink with batch size
PCIe bandwidth drops at large batch sizes
The weights move to disk at batch 144
KV bytes per token grow with the batch size
blocks.explain: Only the weight term is divided by the batch: 47.4 GB / b. The KV term is 727 MB per sequence per step regardless of b. At 144 the KV is 0.73 of the 1.06 GB. Moving attention to the CPU removes that term, which is why FlexGen delegates it.

lessons.title: Finding a prefix across tiers, requests and engines

blocks.md: Back to reuse offloading. Offload tiers reuse the same key the GPU prefix cache uses: a hash of a block's tokens chained with the hash of everything before it. That makes a stored chunk meaningful to *any* request with the same prefix, whether it comes from the same user later, another user sharing a system prompt, or another engine instance reading a shared store. Granularity varies: vLLM's offloaded `block_size` must be a multiple of the GPU block size, and LMCache stores KV in chunks of 256 tokens by default.

Because keys are chained, only a **contiguous prefix** counts. The lookup walks the request's blocks in order, first in HBM, then in the offload tiers, and stops at the first block found nowhere. The code below is a simplified planner in that spirit (real connectors work in tokens, align to block boundaries and batch the lookups).

blocks.title: Planning a request across tiers (simplified)

scenes.caption: An 8-block prompt arrives. Each block is identified by a chained hash of its tokens and all earlier tokens, so h5 can only be valid if h0 to h4 are the same prefix.
First, the ordinary GPU prefix cache: h0 and h1 are in HBM, h2 is not. Two blocks need no transfer at all.
Next, the offload tiers, still walking the prefix in order. h2, h3, h4 come from the CPU tier, h5 only exists in the remote store.
h6 is nowhere, so the walk stops. h7 is sitting in the CPU tier but cannot be used: its KV was computed after a prefix that included h6, and that position must be recomputed first.
Result: 2 GPU hits, 4 loads, 2 blocks of prefill. A cap like vLLM's max_load_tokens would truncate the load list here and push the rest into prefill.

blocks.md: A cached block after a gap is useless for this request. KV at position 7 depends on every earlier token through attention in every layer, so if block 6 must be recomputed, block 7 must be too, even if an identical hash for it were stored. Eviction that removes a middle block silently strands everything after it.

Once the plan is made, transfers are scheduled so the GPU keeps working. SGLang's HiCache shows the whole flow with three tiers: L1 is GPU memory, L2 is host memory private to the instance, and L3 is distributed storage that can be shared across instances (backends include file, Mooncake, 3FS, NIXL and AIBrix; 3FS is DeepSeek's distributed file system and AIBrix is ByteDance's open-source control plane for vLLM).

blocks.title: SGLang HiCache: a request with hits in all three tiers

scenes.caption: Local match first: the HiRadixTree records which tokens sit in L1 and L2, and returns a prefix whose first part is in GPU memory and the rest in host memory.
The tree keeps no L3 metadata, so the scheduler asks the storage backend in real time how much more of the prefix it holds.
If the L3 hit exceeds a threshold (256 tokens by default), a prefetch copies those pages from L3 into local host memory.
The prefetch policy decides how long to wait: best_effort stops as soon as the GPU can run prefill, wait_complete waits for everything, timeout waits up to a limit that grows with hit length.
Everything now local is loaded into GPU memory, overlapping layer N+1's copy with layer N's compute, and prefill runs only on the tokens nobody had.

blocks.md: Sharing across machines is where the remote tier earns its keep. **Mooncake**, the serving platform for Moonshot AI's Kimi, builds a disaggregated KV cache, a pool separated from any one GPU server, out of the otherwise underused CPU DRAM and SSD of the GPU cluster. Its Mooncake Store keeps multiple replicas of hot objects to spread read load and moves data with its Transfer Engine using GPUDirect RDMA, where the network card reads and writes GPU memory directly, across multiple NICs (network interface cards). The same connector interfaces (LMCache, NIXL, Mooncake) also ship KV from a prefill worker to a decode worker in **disaggregated serving**, where prefill (P) runs on one set of GPUs and decode (D) on another, so the prompt's KV must travel between them: offloading and P/D transfer share one connector interface and often one transfer library, though P/D usually sends KV straight from GPU to GPU while offloading parks it in a tier.

A shared tier raises a question a local one does not: how does an engine learn which blocks exist on *other* machines? Systems keep a metadata service separate from the bytes. Mooncake Store's **master service** tracks every node's memory segments and every object's replicas. A writer asks it for space (`PutStart`), copies the bytes straight into another node's memory, then confirms (`PutEnd`); a reader asks where the replicas are (`GetReplicaList`, which also grants a short lease so the object is not evicted mid-read) and reads them directly. The master never carries KV data. LMCache's coordinator plays the same role for a fleet of LMCache servers: servers register with it, and it keeps a key directory with a lookup endpoint, plus pins and per-tenant quotas. HiCache, above, simply asks its L3 backend at lookup time.

blocks.title: Mooncake Store: metadata via the master, bytes peer to peer

scenes.caption: A prefill node finished a chunk and wants to store it under its hash key. The master allocates space on some node and returns where to write.
The bytes go directly to the memory node over the Transfer Engine (RDMA). Only then does the writer tell the master the object is complete and readable.
Another engine with the same prefix asks the master where the object is. The reply grants a lease, so eviction will not free it mid-read.
The reader pulls the bytes straight from the memory node. The master saw three small messages and none of the gigabytes.

blocks.md:
Concurrency is easier than in a general cache because the key is a hash of the content. Two engines that compute the same prefix produce the same bytes under the same key. Mooncake Store's design doc makes the point directly: a key derived from the value makes the value immutable after insertion, so once a `Put` succeeds the object never changes until it is removed. A second writer of the same key has nothing new to add; Mooncake even blocks a second `PutStart` on a key while the first is unfinished, until a 30-second timeout lets it take over from a writer that crashed.

What breaks this is a key that leaves out something the KV depends on. LMCache's object keys carry the model name and accept extra identity tags such as an adapter revision, and vLLM's file tier stores blocks under a directory derived from the model, block size, parallelism layout and dtype (the number format, such as BF16), so changing any of them starts a new namespace instead of serving stale bytes.

Last, routing. A router that knows which instance already holds a prefix can send the request there and turn a remote load into a local hit. The *PagedAttention and prefix caching* course's fleet lesson covers KV events and cache-aware routers; the offload-specific detail is that host-tier blocks count too. vLLM's OffloadingConnector can publish `BlockStored` and `BlockRemoved` events for offloaded blocks (the `self_describing_kv_events` option), so an external index sees what sits in each instance's CPU tier, and the LMCache paper's controller answers a router's `lookup(tokens)` with the instance, the storage device and the number of hit tokens.
Offload tiers are a bigger prefix cache with the same keys. A hit is the longest contiguous prefix found across all tiers; everything after the first gap is prefill.

blocks.question: A request's blocks are h0 to h9. HBM holds h0 to h3. The CPU tier holds h0 to h6 and h8, h9. What gets loaded from CPU, and what is recomputed?
options: Load h4 to h6 and h8, h9; recompute h7
Load h4 to h6; recompute h7, h8, h9
Load nothing; recompute h4 to h9, since the CPU tier has a gap
Load h0 to h6 again from CPU to refresh them; recompute h7 to h9
blocks.explain: The usable prefix stops at the first block that is nowhere: h7. h4 to h6 extend the GPU hit contiguously, so they are loaded. h8 and h9 were computed after a context that includes h7, which must be recomputed, so they are recomputed along with it.

blocks.question: In SGLang HiCache with the best_effort prefetch policy, a 4,000-token L3 hit is only half fetched when the GPU becomes free. What happens?
options: The fetched part is used with the local hits and the rest is computed by prefill
The request waits until all 4,000 tokens arrive
The partial prefetch is discarded and everything is recomputed
The request is moved to another instance that has the data in L2
blocks.explain: best_effort terminates prefetching as soon as the GPU can run prefill. The data already fetched is used together with the local data, and the remaining tokens are prefilled. wait_complete would have waited for all of it.

blocks.question: Two prefill nodes finish the same 4K-token system prompt at the same moment, and both try to store its blocks in a shared Mooncake-style store keyed by chained token hashes (with the model in the key). What is the right outcome?
options: Store both copies under different keys, so neither write is lost
Merge the two versions block by block, keeping the newer values
Discard both, since a race means neither can be trusted
Let one write complete and have the other skip: both computed identical bytes for the same key
blocks.explain: The key is derived from the tokens and model, so both nodes computed the same KV. Whichever Put completes first is correct for every future reader, and the second writer has nothing to add. Mooncake blocks a concurrent PutStart on the same key and treats a completed object as immutable.

lessons.title: Eviction and placement: what stays, what sinks, what is dropped

blocks.md: Every tier is finite, so each one needs an **admission** rule (what gets written in) and an **eviction** rule (what leaves when it is full). Evicting from HBM can mean demoting to host memory; evicting from the bottom tier means the KV is gone and the next request recomputes it.

Most systems default to recency. vLLM's OffloadingConnector takes `eviction_policy` of `lru` (the default) or `arc`; ARC (adaptive replacement cache) keeps a recency list and a frequency list and adapts how much space each gets. LMCache's multiprocess mode offers LRU, ARC and IsolatedLRU (a separate LRU list for each cache salt, each with its own quota; a cache salt is a per-tenant string mixed into the block hash, so only requests carrying the same salt share cached blocks), evicting 20% of allocated memory per cycle once usage passes an 80% watermark. Mooncake Store evicts by lease: at 90% usage it evicts 5% of objects, oldest expired lease first (each lookup extends a lease, so this approximates LRU), and it skips any object under a live **lease** (granted for 10 seconds by default when a client looks it up) so a block is not freed while a client that just looked it up reads it (if the lease expires mid-read, the read fails rather than return freed data).

Admission matters as much. vLLM's `offload_prompt_only` (on by default) offloads prompt blocks and skips decode blocks, and `store_threshold` can require a minimum number of lookups before a block is offloaded. SGLang HiCache chooses among `write_through` (every access is written to the next level), `write_through_selective` (only after access frequency passes a threshold) and `write_back` (written down only when evicted from the level above).

blocks.title: A 3-session host tier: LRU vs queue-aware eviction

scenes.caption: Three sessions fill the 3-slot host tier (a miss means fetching from SSD or recomputing). Both policies agree so far.
Session A returns: a hit for both.
D arrives. LRU evicts B, the least recently used. Look-ahead sees B coming back soon in the queue and evicts C, whose next use is farthest away.
B returns: a miss for LRU, which just threw it away; a hit for look-ahead.
E is a one-off session. LRU evicts A to make room; look-ahead evicts D, which is not needed until much later.
A returns: LRU misses again. Look-ahead hits. Recency is a poor signal when sessions return in a cycle longer than the cache.
B returns. LRU evicted it again at the previous request (C took its slot); look-ahead kept it. At that C, look-ahead missed too and evicted the one-off E.
After 12 requests: LRU 1 hit, look-ahead 5 hits on the same capacity. Simplified: this look-ahead knows the whole future; a real scheduler only sees its queue.

blocks.md: The toy shows why recency fails for multi-turn chat: sessions return in a cycle longer than the cache, so LRU evicts exactly what comes back next. CachedAttention exploits the fact that the serving scheduler *knows* which jobs are queued. It prefetches the KV of waiting jobs from disk to host memory within a look-ahead window, protects sessions inside a look-ahead eviction window, and evicts at the granularity of a whole session, since a conversation's KV is used all together or not at all.

blocks.title: Hit rates reported by CachedAttention (128 GB DRAM, 10 TB SSD)

scenes.caption: With the same hardware, scheduler-aware placement reached an 86% hit rate versus 58% for LRU and 48% for FIFO in the paper's multi-turn evaluation.

blocks.md: Do not evict a prefix's parent before its children. Because keys are chained, removing an early block makes every later block of that prefix unreachable, yet those stranded blocks still occupy space. SGLang's radix tree evicts leaves first for this reason, and Mooncake Store tries to evict a group of related objects (such as the separate K and V tensors of one entry) together, though not atomically: busy members can survive.

Failure modes to watch for in production: the PCIe or network link is shared with other traffic, so measured load bandwidth can be far below the planning number; pinned host memory is reserved up front and competes with everything else on the host; cache keys must include anything that changes the KV (model, weights version, dtype (the number format, such as BF16), LoRA adapter (a small set of extra low-rank weight matrices that fine-tunes the model)), or a hit returns wrong values; and a remote tier adds tail latency (slow outliers among loads), which is why HiCache bounds prefetch waits and vLLM can cap loads per request.

Choose eviction by reuse pattern, not habit. LRU is a fine default; workloads with known future reuse (queued multi-turn sessions, scheduled agent steps) do much better with placement driven by the scheduler.

blocks.question: A chatbot has 1,000 active sessions that each return every 5 minutes, and the host tier holds 600 sessions. Under strict LRU, what hit rate should you expect for returning sessions, and why?
options: About 60%, because the tier holds 60% of sessions
100%, because LRU keeps recently active sessions
About 50%, because LRU and FIFO behave the same here
Close to 0%, because each session is the least recently used by the time it returns, so it was just evicted
blocks.explain: With a cyclic access pattern larger than the cache, LRU evicts the oldest session, which is exactly the next one to return. Every return misses. Admission filtering that keeps a fixed subset resident, a bigger tier (SSD) or scheduler look-ahead all fix this; matching capacity alone does not.

blocks.question: An engineer configures an offload store whose keys are the hash of the token IDs only. They then deploy a new fine-tuned version of the model behind the same store. What goes wrong?
options: Nothing: KV depends only on the tokens
Every lookup misses because the hashes change
Hits return KV computed by the old weights, silently corrupting outputs
The store evicts all old entries automatically on deploy
blocks.explain: K and V are projections of hidden states through the model's weights, so different weights give different KV for the same tokens. Keys must include the model identity (and dtype, adapter, and similar), or stale KV is served as a hit.

lessons.title: Fewer bytes, more hits: KV compression and non-prefix reuse

blocks.md:
Two limits are left over from earlier lessons. Slow tiers lose to recompute because KV is big, and a hit must be a contiguous prefix. LMCache ships one technique for each: **CacheGen** shrinks the stored bytes and **CacheBlend** reuses chunks that are not a prefix.

A tiny example first. An 8K-token prompt of Llama 3 8B has 1 GiB of KV. Read from an object store at 1 GB/s it takes 1,074 ms, while recomputing takes 330 ms, so the tier is useless. Make the bytes about 7 times smaller, as CacheGen does below, and the read takes about 152 ms: now the slow tier wins.

CacheGen (Liu et al., SIGCOMM 2024) encodes KV the way a video codec encodes frames. Three measured properties drive it.

1. Within a layer and channel, nearby tokens have similar values. So it splits the context into groups of 10 tokens, keeps the first (**anchor**) token at 8-bit precision, and stores every other token as a **delta**, its difference from the anchor, which is concentrated near zero.
2. Errors in shallow layers hurt answers more than errors in deep ones. So it quantizes the deltas of the first third of the layers most finely and the last third most coarsely.
3. Values grouped by layer and channel have low entropy. So an **arithmetic coder**, a lossless code that spends fewer bits on frequent symbols, packs the quantized deltas using a probability table profiled offline for each layer and channel.

Decoding runs on the GPU and is pipelined with the transfer of the next chunk.

CacheGen also adapts to the network. It splits a context into chunks (1.5K tokens by default in the paper), encodes each at several quantization levels ahead of time, measures the throughput of the chunk just sent, and picks the level for the next chunk that keeps loading within the TTFT target; if bandwidth collapses it sends the chunk as text and lets the GPU recompute it.

Reported results: KV 3.5 to 4.3x smaller than a quantization baseline at similar quality, and 3.2 to 3.7x lower delay to fetch and process the context. On Mistral-7B with the LongChat dataset, 8-bit KV took 622 MB and CacheGen 176 MB (3.5x), at a quality score of 0.98 against 1.00. Since 8-bit is half of BF16, that is about 7x smaller than the BF16 KV this course has been loading.

blocks.title: 8K-token prompt, Llama 3 8B: load time at three KV sizes

scenes.caption: BF16 KV, as in the reload-or-recompute lesson: every tier but the object store beats the 330 ms prefill.
8-bit KV halves every load. The object store still needs 537 ms, more than recomputing.
CacheGen-level compression, about 7x smaller than BF16: the object store now loads in 152 ms and beats prefill. Decoding time is assumed hidden behind the transfer, as CacheGen pipelines it.

blocks.tex: B^{\ast} = \frac{n\, b_{kv}\, F}{c \cdot \text{FLOPs}(n)}: \quad 3.26 \;(c=1),\quad 1.63 \;(c=2),\quad 0.46 \;(c \approx 7) \text{ GB/s at } n = 8192
blocks.caption: The break-even bandwidth from the reload-or-recompute lesson, with stored bytes divided by a compression ratio c. Any tier faster than B* should be read. Compression lowers the bar by exactly c.

blocks.md: Compression is not free. CacheGen is lossy (0.98 vs 1.00 above), so measure answer quality, and its decoder needs GPU time that must stay hidden behind the transfer. Quantizing KV that stays in HBM is a separate topic; here the goal is fewer bytes on a slow link.

Now the prefix rule. In retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) a prompt looks like [system][chunk A][chunk B][chunk C][question], and the next query retrieves the same chunks in a different order, or a different mix. With chained hashes only the leading run of identical tokens hits: the system prompt and at most the first chunk.

Earlier systems reused chunks anyway. Prompt Cache (Gim et al.) has the user declare reusable **prompt modules** in a schema, gives each module its own range of position IDs, and concatenates their precomputed attention states. This **full KV reuse** keeps positions correct but ignores **cross-attention**, CacheBlend's name for attention between chunks (not the encoder-decoder cross-attention of the Transformer course): a chunk's KV was computed without seeing the chunks before it, so tokens whose meaning depends on an earlier chunk do not reflect it, and answers that need facts from two chunks can go wrong.

CacheBlend (Yao et al., EuroSys 2025) reuses each chunk's KV wherever it lands and recomputes a few tokens per layer to restore cross-attention.

1. Fix positions. With rotary position embedding (RoPE), moving a key to a new position is one multiplication by a rotation matrix, a cheap one-time step.
2. At the first layer, recompute every token and measure each token's **KV deviation**, the distance between its reused KV and its freshly computed KV.
3. Keep the tokens with the largest deviation (**HKVD**, high-KV-deviation tokens), recompute only those at the next layer, and narrow the set slightly at each layer. This works because tokens that deviate at one layer tend to deviate at the next.

In the paper about 10 to 15% of tokens carried most of the deviation, and recomputing 15% kept quality close to a full prefill. Compute is proportional to the tokens selected.

blocks.title: Four cached chunks, reused in a new order (toy, 5 tokens each)

scenes.caption: Chunks A to D were retrieved before, and each chunk's KV was computed on its own and stored. The new query retrieves them in the order C, A, D, B.
Prefix caching walks from the first token: C1 is not where A1 was, so not one chunk hits. All 20 tokens are recomputed.
Full KV reuse loads every chunk with positions fixed. Fast, but A's tokens never attended to C, and D's never attended to C or A.
CacheBlend, layer 1: recompute all tokens once to see whose KV changes when the real preceding chunks are present. That is 1/32 of a full prefill for a 32-layer model.
Layers 2 to 32: only the 3 tokens with the largest deviation (15%) are recomputed; the rest use the loaded KV. Toy positions; real HKVD tokens are wherever cross-attention matters.

blocks.code:
# CacheBlend-style estimate on Llama 3 8B (course cost model, 400 TFLOPS, 50 GB/s DRAM tier).
P, L, d, F, B = 6.979e9, 32, 4096, 400e12, 50e9
bkv = 2 * 32 * 8 * 128 * 2                     # 131,072 bytes per token
def prefill(n, start=0):                       # FLOPs for tokens start..n-1, causal
    m = n - start
    return 2*P*m + 2*L*d*(n*n - start*start)
chunks, q, r = 4 * 512, 32, 0.15               # 4 retrieved chunks, a 32-token question
n = chunks + q
full = prefill(n)
prefix = prefill(n, 512)                       # at best the first chunk is a cached prefix
load_ms = chunks * bkv / B * 1e3
sel = round(r * chunks)
# layer 1 recomputes every chunk token to find deviations; layers 2..32 recompute r of them
blend = (1/L + r*(L-1)/L) * prefill(chunks) + prefill(n, chunks)
reuse = prefill(n, chunks)                     # full KV reuse: only the question
ms = lambda f: f / F * 1e3
print(f"recomputed tokens per layer at {r:.0%}: {sel} of {chunks}")
print(f"full prefill      {ms(full):6.1f} ms")
print(f"prefix caching    {ms(prefix):6.1f} ms (first chunk hit at best)")
print(f"full KV reuse     {max(load_ms, 0) + ms(reuse):6.1f} ms (load {load_ms:.1f} + question {ms(reuse):.1f})")
lay_load, lay_comp = load_ms / L, ms(blend) / L
print(f"CacheBlend        compute {ms(blend):.1f} ms, load {load_ms:.1f} ms, "
      f"per layer {lay_comp:.2f} vs {lay_load:.2f} ms")
print(f"  pipelined TTFT  {max(load_ms, ms(blend)) + min(load_ms, ms(blend))/L:6.1f} ms")

blocks.md:
Output:

```
recomputed tokens per layer at 15%: 307 of 2048
full prefill        75.4 ms
prefix caching      57.4 ms (first chunk hit at best)
full KV reuse        6.6 ms (load 5.4 + question 1.2)
CacheBlend        compute 14.3 ms, load 5.4 ms, per layer 0.45 vs 0.17 ms
  pipelined TTFT    14.5 ms
```

Four retrieved chunks of 512 tokens in a new order plus a 32-token question. CacheBlend recomputes 307 of the 2,048 chunk tokens per layer; loading the chunks' 268 MB from DRAM pipelines with that compute layer by layer, so TTFT is about 14.5 ms against 57.4 ms for the best case of prefix caching. This idealized model gives 4x over prefix caching and 5.2x over full prefill; on real hardware the paper measured 2.2 to 3.3x lower TTFT than full KV recompute.

The same overlap logic picks the recompute ratio and the storage device. CacheBlend's loading controller chooses a ratio whose recompute time per layer hides behind the load time per layer. For Llama-7B with a 4K context, recomputing 15% took 3 ms per layer while loading a layer from NVMe took 16 ms, so recompute was free; for Llama-70B it was 7 ms of recompute against 4 ms of loading, so it was not. Given a fixed ratio, the controller can instead pick the cheapest device whose load time still hides the recompute. LMCache exposes CacheBlend as a server option ([docs](https://docs.lmcache.ai/kv_cache_optimizations/cacheblend.html)): `lmcache server --engine-type blend`.

Compression lowers the break-even bandwidth by the compression ratio, which can turn a slow tier from useless to worth reading. Position-independent reuse turns reordered RAG chunks into hits. Both trade a little accuracy, so measure answer quality, not only TTFT.

blocks.question: A RAG service caches each retrieved chunk's KV separately, fixes RoPE positions when chunks are concatenated in a new order, and skips all recomputation. Answers that need facts from two chunks get worse. Why?
options: The RoPE fix shifts every key by the wrong angle
Each chunk's KV was computed without attending to the chunks now before it, so cross-chunk dependencies are missing
Chained hashes collide when chunks are reordered
The question's KV is loaded from the cache instead of computed
blocks.explain: Positions are fixed correctly, but KV at every layer after the first depends on what each token attended to. A chunk computed alone never saw its new neighbours, so its later-layer KV lacks that context. CacheBlend recomputes the few tokens whose KV deviates most to restore it.

blocks.question: You serve Llama 3 8B with 8K-token prompts on a GPU sustaining 400 TFLOPS and keep cold KV in an object store that delivers 1 GB/s. Which stored format makes reading beat recomputing?
options: BF16, as computed
8-bit quantized KV
None: at 1 GB/s recomputing always wins
A CacheGen-style encoding about 7x smaller than BF16
blocks.explain: Recompute is 330 ms. BF16 needs 1,074 ms and 8-bit 537 ms, both slower. At about 7x smaller the read is 152 ms, faster than prefill, because break-even bandwidth falls from 3.26 to about 0.46 GB/s.

lessons.title: Hands-on: configure an offload tier and measure it

blocks.md:
This lesson turns the course into a procedure: configure a CPU tier, run a workload that needs it, and check what you measure against the cost model. The serving commands need an NVIDIA GPU and were **not run here**; every measured number below comes from a published run, and the simulator at the end runs on any CPU.

Start with sizing, using numbers you already have. Llama 3 8B stores 128 KiB per token, so 40 GB of free HBM holds about 305,000 tokens: 37 chat histories of 8K. Two hundred users whose histories grow to 8K need about 215 GB. That is the regime where a host tier matters: more active sessions than HBM holds, fewer than DRAM holds.

blocks.code:
# Not run here: needs an NVIDIA GPU (written on a machine without one).
# vLLM's built-in CPU tier: 200 GB of pinned host memory, LRU eviction.
vllm serve meta-llama/Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct \
  --kv-transfer-config '{
    "kv_connector": "OffloadingConnector",
    "kv_role": "kv_both",
    "kv_connector_extra_config": {
      "cpu_bytes_to_use": 200000000000,
      "eviction_policy": "lru"
    }
  }'

# Alternative, also not run here: LMCache as a separate server
# (multiprocess mode; chunks default to 256 tokens).
lmcache server --l1-size-gb 200 --eviction-policy LRU
vllm serve meta-llama/Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct --kv-transfer-config \
  '{"kv_connector": "LMCacheMPConnector", "kv_role": "kv_both"}'
blocks.caption: Configurations from the vLLM KV offloading guide and the LMCache quickstart (not run here). Flags change between releases; check the docs for your version.

blocks.md: Three settings matter most. `cpu_bytes_to_use` is pinned host memory, counted across all workers of the engine, not per GPU. vLLM's guide says to make it larger than the aggregate GPU KV cache, because blocks are copied out as soon as they are computed: a smaller CPU tier only mirrors what HBM already holds and adds no hits. `block_size` (a multiple of the GPU block size) sets the transfer unit: larger chunks mean larger, more efficient I/Os but coarser lookups. And `eviction_policy` is `lru` or `arc`, as in the eviction lesson.

Then measure. Run the same workload against vLLM alone and with the tier: `vllm bench serve` reports TTFT percentiles, and LMCache's `lmcache bench engine` has a long-document Q&A workload that sizes its document set from a target KV volume ([benchmarking guide](https://docs.lmcache.ai/getting_started/benchmarking.html)). Record three things.

- TTFT per turn, at p50 and p90, not only the mean.
- The tier's hit rate, in tokens. vLLM's `vllm:prompt_tokens_cached_by_source` splits cached prompt tokens by the tier that supplied them (`device` for HBM, `host` for DRAM, `disk`), next to the GPU-only `vllm:prefix_cache_hits` from the PagedAttention course. LMCache exports `lmcache_mp.lookup_hit` over `lmcache_mp.lookup_requested` and counts only the contiguous prefix hit.
- Achieved load bandwidth: bytes loaded divided by load time. Compare it with the 50 GB/s you planned with.

What to expect, from vLLM's published runs on one H100 with Llama-3.1-8B (GPU prefix caching disabled to isolate CPU hits). A single request's TTFT fell by 2x to 22x depending on prompt length; at 100K tokens their chart shows about 6.8 s to compute against about 0.3 s to load. Moving 100K x 128 KiB = 13.1 GB in about 0.3 s is roughly 43 GB/s, close to the planning number.

Their throughput test sent 10,000 unique 512-token prefill requests at a controlled CPU hit rate. Throughput rose from about 42,500 tokens/s with no hits to about 389,000 with all hits, where KV moved at about 51 GB/s (389,000 tokens/s times 131,072 bytes; the chart's right axis shows about 47.5, the same rate in binary gigabytes). The curve between follows a simple model closely.

blocks.caption: A fraction h of tokens is loaded (1/R seconds each) and the rest computed (1/C each). Throughput is the harmonic mix. C and R are the measured endpoints.

blocks.title: Throughput vs CPU hit rate: model and vLLM's H100 measurements

scenes.caption: Points are read off vLLM's chart (approximate). The serial model tracks them within about 6 percent; perfect overlap of loads and compute would predict about 425K at 90% hits instead of the measured 218K.
The same tier behind a link shared down to 3 GB/s: R falls to about 23K tokens/s, below the compute rate, and more hits make throughput worse. Measure bandwidth before trusting hit rate.
A GPU that computes twice as fast (C = 85K) gains less from the same tier: the load rate did not change, so the gap between computing and loading narrowed.

blocks.code:
import random
P, L, d, F, KV = 6.979e9, 32, 4096, 400e12, 131072  # Llama 3 8B
def pf(n, s=0):                       # prefill ms for tokens s..n-1
    return (2*P*(n-s) + 2*L*d*(n*n-s*s)) / F * 1e3
def run(hbm_gb, dram_gb, bw=50e9, users=200, turns=8, new=512):
    cap = [hbm_gb*1e9/KV, dram_gb*1e9/KV]   # capacity in tokens
    tier = [{}, {}]                          # LRU order: user -> tokens
    hist = [0]*users; turn = hist[:]
    order = [u for u in range(users) for _ in range(turns)]
    random.Random(0).shuffle(order)
    hits = dict(hbm=0, dram=0, miss=0); per = [[] for _ in range(turns)]
    for u in order:
        h = hist[u]
        if h == 0 or u in tier[0]: k, t = "hbm", pf(h+new, h)
        elif u in tier[1]:
            del tier[1][u]
            a, b = h*KV/bw*1e3, pf(h+new, h)  # layer-wise
            k, t = "dram", max(a, b) + min(a, b)/L
        else: k, t = "miss", pf(h+new)
        hits[k] += h > 0; per[turn[u]].append(t); turn[u] += 1
        hist[u] = h + 2*new   # question plus answer
        tier[0].pop(u, None); tier[0][u] = hist[u]
        for i in (0, 1):   # demote LRU downward
            while sum(tier[i].values()) > cap[i]:
                v = next(iter(tier[i])); size = tier[i].pop(v)
                if i == 0 and cap[1]: tier[1][v] = size
    n = sum(hits.values())
    print({k: f"{x/n:.0%}" for k, x in hits.items()},
          [round(sum(p)/len(p)) for p in per])
run(40, 0)            # HBM prefix cache only
run(40, 512)          # plus 512 GB DRAM at 50 GB/s
run(40, 512, bw=3e9)  # DRAM behind a shared link

Simplified: whole sessions move between tiers, a session reaches DRAM only when HBM evicts it (vLLM copies blocks out at once), the GPU is otherwise idle, and TTFT excludes queueing. In this simulator, two hundred users return in random order to a 40 GB HBM cache that holds under a fifth of them. With HBM alone, 61% of their returns miss and TTFT climbs to 256 ms by turn 8. A 512 GB DRAM tier turns every miss into a load and holds TTFT near 23 ms. Behind a link shared down to 3 GB/s, the same hits are slightly *worse* than recomputing by turn 8 (262 vs 256 ms): a real planner compares load and recompute per request.

blocks.md:
A sizing and topology checklist before you trust a deployment:

- **Pinned memory.** The CPU tier is reserved up front and competes with everything else on the host. Eight GPUs with 40 GB of KV each need a tier well above 320 GB to add hits.
- **Shared links.** Find which GPUs, NICs and SSDs share a PCIe switch; simultaneous reloads split its uplink, as in the DGX-2 example of the first lesson.
- **NUMA** (non-uniform memory access: on a multi-socket server each CPU has its own memory, and reaching another socket's is slower). Keep the host buffer on the CPU socket the GPU is attached to. vLLM's docs note that its simple CPU offload connector's caches follow the worker's NUMA policy (for example `--numa-bind`); a buffer on the other socket makes every copy cross the CPU interconnect.

- **SSD tier: bandwidth at your I/O size.** Divide bandwidth by chunk size to get the reads per second the drive must sustain. For Llama 3 8B a 16-token vLLM block holding all layers is 2 MiB, about 2,900 reads/s at 6 GB/s; a 256-token LMCache chunk is 32 MiB, about 180 reads/s. vLLM's older layout split a block per layer into 32 KB pieces, which at the same rate means about 183,000 reads/s; vLLM's team reported that merging layers into one block raised offloading throughput by an order of magnitude.
- **GPUDirect Storage.** With an NVMe tier, GDS lets the SSD's DMA engine write into GPU memory without a bounce buffer in host memory ([overview](https://docs.nvidia.com/gpudirect-storage/overview-guide/index.html)), the dashed direct path in the first lesson's diagram.

Finally, the economics. Provider prompt caching prices this same trade. Anthropic's API bills cache reads at a fraction of the base input price (0.1x is the standard multiplier, lower on some models), 5-minute cache writes at 1.25x and 1-hour writes at 2x. A longer time to live is a request to keep KV somewhere for longer, which in serving terms means a bigger or deeper tier. The *PagedAttention and prefix caching* course's last lesson shows how these APIs mark a cacheable prefix.

A high hit rate is not a win by itself. Check achieved bandwidth and TTFT per turn too: a tier behind a congested link can hit 100% and still be slower than recomputing, and a tier smaller than the GPU cache can report hits that HBM would have served anyway.
Size the tier from KV bytes per token and the number of active sessions, then verify three numbers against the cost model: hit rate, achieved load bandwidth and TTFT per turn.

blocks.question: After deploying a DRAM tier you measure 8 GB/s of load bandwidth instead of the 50 GB/s you planned. Which set of causes is most likely?
options: Pageable host buffers or many small transfers, the PCIe uplink shared with other GPUs or a NIC, or a buffer on the far NUMA socket
The GPU is too fast, HBM is too small, and the model is too large
LRU eviction, too many sessions, and prompts that are too long
BF16 instead of FP8, a mismatched tokenizer, and short prompts
blocks.explain: Bandwidth is set by the path: pinned memory and large, contiguous transfers are needed to approach link speed (vLLM's 32 KB-per-layer layout was far slower than 2 MB blocks); a switch uplink is split among devices that use it at once; and a host buffer on the remote socket crosses the CPU interconnect. The other options affect hit rate or compute, not link bandwidth.

blocks.question: A GPU holds 40 GB of KV cache. You enable vLLM's OffloadingConnector with `cpu_bytes_to_use` set to 30 GB. How many extra hits should the CPU tier add?
options: About 75% more, since 30 GB is 75% of HBM
Twice as many, since the cache doubles in size
It depends only on the eviction policy
Almost none: blocks are copied out as soon as they are computed, so a tier smaller than HBM only mirrors blocks HBM still holds
blocks.explain: Offloading is immediate, so the CPU tier holds copies of recent blocks, most of which are still in HBM. Only a tier larger than the aggregate GPU KV cache keeps blocks HBM has already evicted. vLLM's tuning guide says exactly this.
